introduction: The guide holds that creation has neither beginning nor end, that space is without limit and the worlds without number, that our earth is a grain in it, and that the mind cannot form a clear idea of any of this and yet can know that it must be so, because a Creator without a creation is unthinkable. Its sixty quotations are read here with sixty from elsewhere. The psalms and prophets speak of stars that cannot be numbered, of a thousand years as yesterday, of a God who inhabits eternity and does not change; the Qur’an of days of a thousand and of fifty thousand years; Plato of time as the moving image of eternity; Augustine of how little he can say what time is; Heraclitus, the Gita and Marcus Aurelius of a world that always was and comes round again. Pascal is frightened by the same infinite spaces. Genesis ends creation on the seventh day, and Jesus and Peter expect heaven and earth to pass away. The psalm’s unmoving earth marks how much the picture of the heavens has changed, and Blake, Hamlet and Pascal ask where infinity leaves the one who contemplates it.
questions: The guide argues that a Creator must always have had a creation, so creation has no beginning. Does the argument persuade you, and what does it assume?
Jesus and Peter speak of heaven and earth passing away, and Genesis of a finished creation. How does the guide read such passages, and how else have they been read?
Pascal is frightened by infinite space, the psalmist is moved to praise, and Blake finds infinity in a grain of sand. Which response is nearest your own?
Augustine knows what time is until he is asked. What, in your own experience, comes closest to an intimation of eternity?
The guide says the human intellect cannot form a clear conception of infinity. What is the use of thinking about what cannot be conceived?
If the earth is a grain of dust among numberless worlds, what follows for how human beings should regard themselves and one another?

outside.why: The Rig Veda's hymn of creation asks who knows whence it came into being, and leaves the answer with the highest.
Pascal wrote that the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightened him. Why does infinite space gladden one reader of scripture and terrify another?
Jesus says that in his Father's house are many mansions, and that he would have said so if it were not.
After naming the creatures people know and use, the Qur'an adds that God createth that which ye know not.
Isaiah counts the nations as a drop of a bucket and the small dust of the balance.
Blake would see a world in a grain of sand and hold infinity in the palm of the hand. Is the smallness of the earth a reason for humility, or is infinity as near as a grain of dust?
Darwin writes of endless forms most beautiful that have been, and are being, evolved from so simple a beginning.
Lucretius makes it a first principle that nothing from nothing ever yet was born.
Plotinus says that the One, lacking nothing, has overflowed, and its exuberance has produced the new.
The psalm says that by the word of the Lord were the heavens made.
The Lord asks Job: where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?
Jesus says that heaven and earth shall pass away. How is a creation without end to be read beside a scripture that expects an end?
Peter's letter expects a day when the heavens pass away and the elements melt with fervent heat. Is that the end of the physical world, or of something else?
John sees a new heaven and a new earth, the first having passed away.
The Preacher says that whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever.
Jesus claims a priority that is not measured in years: before Abraham was, I am.
The Qur'an says: as We began the first creation, We shall repeat it.
The psalm says: before the mountains were brought forth, from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
The Preacher says that to every thing there is a season, a time to plant and a time to pluck up.
Plato's Timaeus says that the maker resolved to have a moving image of eternity, and this image we call time.
The name given to Moses has no tense but the present: I AM THAT I AM.
Revelation names him Alpha and Omega, which is, and which was, and which is to come.
Augustine asks what time is, and answers: if no one ask of me, I know; if I wish to explain, I know not.
Kant says that two things fill the mind with ever new awe, the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
The psalm says that the world is established, that it cannot be moved. What did it cost, and what did it give, to learn that the old picture of an enclosed heaven was wrong?

Hamlet says he could be bounded in a nutshell and count himself a king of infinite space, were it not that he has bad dreams. Is infinity a fact about the universe, or about the mind that conceives it?
Abram is brought out and told to look toward heaven and tell the stars, if he be able to number them.
Jeremiah says that the host of heaven cannot be numbered, neither the sand of the sea measured.
The psalm says that he telleth the number of the stars, and that his understanding is infinite.
Plato's Timaeus watches the elements pass into one another, water becoming stone and earth by condensation.
Paul says of the one who is before all things that by him all things consist.
The psalm says that the heavens declare the glory of God, and night unto night shows knowledge.
Keats feels like some watcher of the skies when a new planet swims into his ken.
Aristotle's first cause is not dependent on what it moves: it moves all things as being loved.
Heraclitus says that this world was ever, is now and ever shall be.
Genesis says that the heavens and the earth were finished, and that on the seventh day God rested. How does a creation that was finished stand with a creation that has always been?
Jesus says that the divine work has never stopped: my Father worketh hitherto, and I work.
The Qur'an says that all in the heavens and the earth entreat Him, and that every day He exercises power.
The psalm says that the heavens shall be changed like a vesture, but thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end.
Malachi hears the ground of an unchanging sovereignty: I am the Lord, I change not.
Isaiah speaks of the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy.
The Qur'an calls him the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward.
The Throne Verse calls God the Alive, the Eternal, whom neither slumber nor sleep overtakes.
Marcus Aurelius says that all things from eternity are of like forms and come round in a circle.
The psalm says that a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past.
Krishna says that at the close of each age all things return to his being, and at its beginning issue forth again.
The Gita says that the spirit was never born and shall cease to be never.
Solomon says that heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain God.
Hamlet says that there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in philosophy.
Hebrews says that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
The Qur'an says that if the sea became ink for the words of the Lord, the sea would be used up first.
Lamentations says that his compassions fail not: they are new every morning.
Isaiah says: lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, and calleth them all by names.
The Qur'an speaks of an ascent in a Day whereof the span is fifty thousand years.
The psalm gives thanks unto the Lord, for he is good, and his mercy endureth for ever.
Peter's letter says that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
The Preacher watches the sun arise and go down and hasten to the place where he arose.
The Preacher says that God has made every thing beautiful in his time, and that no man can find out the work from beginning to end.
Lao Tzu speaks of something undefined and complete that came into existence before Heaven and Earth.
Pascal calls man a nothing in comparison with the infinite, and an all in comparison with the nothing. Where does a creation without beginning or end leave the one who thinks about it?
